title: Self-defence or 'brutal' killing: lawyers give closing arguments in Vandewater trial
subtitle: Tyler Vandewater stared straight ahead from the prisoner's box during much of his murder trial. He did not appear so stoic as the trial drew to a close on Wednesday.
article: Tyler Vandewater stared straight ahead from the prisoner's box during much of his murder trial. He did not appear so stoic as the trial drew to a close on Wednesday.

The 31-year-old often raised his shoulders, dropped his head to his chest and sipped water during closing arguments in his second-degree murder trial over the June 2017 death of his Saskatchewan Penitentiary cellmate, 37-year-old Christopher Van Camp.

Vandewater has testified that he was acting in self-defence, that a paranoid Van Camp lunged at him with a homemade blade before Vandewater pushed him back, and that the ensuing 60- to 90-second struggle turned fatal before he realized it.
Crown prosecutor Linh Lê said she has "concerns" about elements of Vandewater's self-defence argument, describing his claim that his actions were reasonable under the circumstances as a "fail."
Last week, forensic pathologist Shaun Ladham said Van Camp had 26 wounds to his face and 25 wounds on his upper back. He died of blood loss and suffered a collapsed lung.
Vandewater had light scratches on his side.
Defence lawyer Brian Pfefferle asked Justice Brian Scherman to consider Vandewater's circumstances.
"We've got someone who's literally locked in a cage with another human being," he said.

Vandewater and Van Camp lived in the facility's C-Range, which Vandewater said primarily houses members of the Terror Squad gang and its associates. If an inmate gives information to the guards, he testified, he is considered a "snitch" and could get stabbed at any moment.

Pfefferle emphasized that unwritten rule among the inmates doesn't excuse them from obeying the law, but said Vandewater has "spent the better part of his life where violence is deemed to be prevalent ... He's got scars on his body to prove (it)."

Both Lê and Scherman raised concerns about one particular aspect of Vandewater's testimony: he said an unknown inmate, whom he'd only identify by the nickname "Slim," gave him permission to tell his story in court.
"Who else is telling him what to say, how to say it?" Lê said.

Because of Vandewater's past offences, she also argued that "this is not someone who's never been engaged in a fight." Vandewater testified that he refused to let Van Camp get up during the altercation because "all it takes is one shot" to get killed.

"He said all it takes is one stab and he decided to give 63," she said. The 26 wounds on Van Camp's face, however, were not all from stabbings. Vandewater said he also "stomped" on his cellmate's head.
Vandewater may have started out acting in self-defence, but "it was his decision to finish the job," Lê argued.
"Are we the court that allows the brutal killing of a cellmate when there are other options?"
Pfefferle argued that his client couldn't have passed a note to a guard or hit the emergency button in their cell when Van Camp was still in the cell with a weapon.
He said much of the evidence presented by witnesses, except for Vandewater, is unreliable.
"The only person who told what happened in that cell is the gentleman sitting behind me," Pfefferle said.
Scherman is expected to deliver his verdict on March 5.
